chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from Abdullah ibn al-Husayn, from al-Salt al-Khazzaz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
When the crescent moon sets before the twilight (afterglow), then it is for its [first] night; and when it sets after the twilight, then it is for two nights [the second night].

key_terms.الشفق: Twilight/afterglow; the reddish or white light remaining in the western sky after sunset. Jurists distinguish between the red twilight (shafaq al-ahmar) and the white twilight (shafaq al-abyad)
key_terms.الهلال: The crescent moon; specifically the new moon crescent seen on the first or second day of the lunar month

ai.seo_question: How is the night of the crescent moon determined in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes a practical jurisprudential criterion for determining whether a newly sighted crescent moon belongs to the first or second night of the lunar month. The rule is: if the hilal (new crescent) disappears before the evening twilight (shafaq) has faded, it is counted as the moon of the first night; if it disappears after the twilight, it counts as the second night's moon. This ruling is directly relevant to the determination of the beginning of Ramadan and other Islamic months, where witnessing the crescent is required. The early jurists applied this criterion to distinguish a moon that had already been in the sky for one day (hence setting before the shafaq, being very young) from one that was two days old.
